cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Shall we go through the notes we’ve made from our research into loneliness now, Dev?

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: OK, Tamara. It’s been a real eye-opener. I had no idea that loneliness has been increasing steadily for the last 20 years.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: I know. And it’s the same all over the world. The downside of a modern lifestyle, I guess.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: Did you come to any conclusions about what the reasons for the increase are?

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Well, I’d assumed it was mainly an issue for the elderly, but in fact it’s something which affects young people just as much.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: So nothing really to do with longer lifespans. What about social media? In my case, far from

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: making me feel isolated, it actually does the opposite. it?

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: It definitely does more good than harm.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: I’d say loneliness has a lot to do with the way cities are designed.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: People living in high flats with not much opportunity to speak to their neighbours

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: I think you right

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Another possible reason is that people are having fewer children and don live in large extended family groups.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: But in this country anyway, that all changed decades ago. And yet loneliness is a more recent problem.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: I suppose so. A more plausible explanation is that people are having to move around for work and often end up living miles away from their family and friends.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: That’s true.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Looking at the studies on health risks and loneliness, there are claims that loneliness has as much impact as smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: Or similar to the risks caused by obesity. But I’m not sure there’s enough evidence for some of these claims.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Well, what about that one in Finland, which showed that loneliness increased the risk of cancer by about 10%? And those findings have been supported by other studies too.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: You’re right about that one. I was actually thinking of the studies on dementia. Some found no association between loneliness and dementia, and others found the opposite.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Not exactly reliable, then. There’s been a lot of research on cardiovascular disease and whether loneliness contributes to that.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: Yes, I read that it was hard to reach a judgment, as the definition of loneliness varied quite a lot, and the responses from participants were too subjective.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: But there’s no doubt that loneliness contributes to a weakened immune system.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Unquestionably. The data on that is sound.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: What did you think about the evolutionary theory of loneliness?

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Well I thought the idea that loneliness evolved because it motivated people to be with other people is quite convincing. Survival often depended on group cooperation.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: But I don think there is enough evidence to claim that there must be a group of neurons in our brains which influence social behaviour by making us feel bad when we’re alone.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: There are a few studies which support the theory, but not conclusively enough. More evidence is needed.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: And anyway, this theory’s not really useful when it comes to solving the problem of loneliness today.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: TAMARA True.
Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: Should we look at the relationship between loneliness and mental health now?

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: OK. So, loneliness and depression are clearly related and that’s been recognised by various governments around the world. But unlike depression, loneliness has no recognised clinical form.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: There’s no available diagnosis or effective treatment and that’s not likely to change.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: I don’t think so either I was thinking we should start our presentation with an example from our own experience I like to talk about how lonely I was when I started university being away from home for the first time and all that

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: Good idea. Everyone will be able to relate to that although a lot of students were probably too embarrassed to admit to it.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Yeah. We could discuss ways of dealing with loneliness as well, like just talking to strangers.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: Loads of studies have shown that interactions with shop assistants and bar staff make people feel more optimistic and relaxed.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: I don’t know about that, but it must make people feel more connected with their community.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: True, although you need to be a certain kind of person to be able to just strike up a conversation.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Good point.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: We should say something about solitude and how being alone and being lonely aren’t the same thing.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: It’s strange the way some people can’t stand being by themselves while others love it.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: Yeah, the research shows a certain amount of solitude is beneficial for wellbeing, which I appreciate, but being alone isn’t something I actually like.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: I’d never choose to go on holiday alone, for example.

cues.speaker: TAMARA
cues.text: Me neither.

cues.speaker: DEV
cues.text: Well, let’s not… you
